title: Who will carry Rangers' goal threat after 'significant' Shankland injury?
description: Rangers captain Lawrence Shankland is set for a spell on the sidelines after picking up a "significant" hamstring injury in Saturday's Scottish Premiership victory over Motherwell.
fullText:
Watch Rangers v Motherwell highlights

Just when Lawrence Shankland was finding his form as a Rangers striker and captain, rediscovering his lethal touch in front of goal, he was struck down by injury.

With barely five minutes gone in Saturday's 1-0 victory over Motherwell, Shankland grasped his hamstring and immediately signalled to the bench that he was done.

It looked bad at the time, and manager Derek McInnes confirmed as much.

"It looks quite significant," he told BBC Scotland after the game. "It's a similar injury we think that he had at Hearts last January.

"We'll get the scan done on Monday and see how it looks then rather than speculating. It's disappointing because he was leading the line and scoring a few goals in the last couple of games.

"There were more positives than negatives from today, but that was a negative."

Three wins in row for Rangers as Naderi goal downs Motherwell

Rangers striker Kelsy's colourful career - aged just 22

Visit our Rangers page for all the latest news, analysis and fan views

After three goals in the previous two games - decisive contributions in wins at Aberdeen and Falkirk - Shankland's injury comes at a particularly bad time, for him and for Rangers.

With fellow striker Youssef Chermiti expected to be out for a lengthy period after suffering anterior cruciate ligament damage against Hibernian last month, Rangers are now left without their two leading strikers.

They were good value for their win over Motherwell, but with the number of chances they created, it should have been more comfortable.

"If Lawrence Shankland was on the pitch throughout, he'd be walking away with a couple of goals," former Rangers midfielder Andy Halliday said on Sportsound.

"Rangers were a bit toothless at the top end of the pitch given the chances they created, but well worth their victory."

Ryan Naderi scored the only goal of the game, capitalising on a shocking blunder from Motherwell keeper Alex Paulsen to roll the ball into an empty net.

The big striker is a willing worker, but can he deliver the sort of goalscoring numbers that Shankland has consistently produced in the Scottish Premiership?

Naderi scored three goals in his 11 games last season after joining Rangers in January, two of which came in the 8-0 Scottish Cup rout of Queen's Park.

The German has scored three in eight appearances this season - one fewer than Shankland's four goals in 10 games.

Since joining Rangers, he has averaged a goal every 189 minutes. That figure is 146 minutes for Shankland stretching back to the start of last season for Hearts.

The only striker on Rangers' books whose stats compare favourably with Shankland is Bojan Miovski, who averages a goal every 148 minutes. However, the former Aberdeen favourite has found it difficult to get a consistent run in the side.

Kevin Kelsy will come into the mix following his arrival from MLS side Portland Timbers.

The Venezuelan had a golden opportunity to announce himself on his debut against Motherwell when presented with a big chance following Jake Girdwood-Reich's error, but showed little composure as he failed to find the target from 10 yards.

Of course it is far too early to rush to judgement on Kelsy's ability to fill the Shankland void, but 13 goals in his last 46 games – averaging one every 190 minutes – would suggest Rangers have not signed an out-and-out goalscorer.

"Rangers missed too many chances, particularly in that second half," former Ibrox midfielder Ian McCall said on Sportsound. "Shankland's injury is a worry because Kelsy and Naderi don't look natural finishers."

After some of the unimaginative, uninspiring and ultimately unsuccessful attacking play his side served up in those early European qualifiers, the encouraging sign for McInnes in the victory over Motherwell was his team's ability to attack with more purpose and create numerous clear-cut chances.

With Shankland now set for a spell on the sidelines, Rangers need someone to step up and take them.

title: No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive?
description: There will be no British interest in the second week of another Grand Slam at the US Open - but is it all doom and gloom?
fullText:
For the fourth time in five majors, there will be no British interest in the second week when the US Open moves into the latter stages.

Underwhelming performances at this year's Australian Open, French Open and Wimbledon led to a series of inquests into what was going wrong.

But there is not quite the same sense of doom and gloom, despite everyone being wiped out after the second round in New York.

"Do I think there could be an inquest? I always think there's things that British tennis could do better. So yes, definitely," said British women's number three Francesca Jones.

"Do I think it's something that's concerning? No, not at all.

"The level is getting better and everyone is dangerous on their day."

With the Grand Slam season now over for the singles players, BBC Sport analyses the positives and negatives in British tennis.

Arthur Fery's extraordinary run to the Wimbledon semi-finals is the clear highlight.

The 24-year-old was ranked 114th in the world and needed a wildcard to play at the All England Club, but took full advantage to produce a performance which nobody could have predicted.

Fery was the only player to reach the second week at a Slam this year and has been heralded by British tennis bosses as proof their talent development pathway is working.

Nine Britons competing in the US Open main-draw singles - the most since 1981- is also highlighted as a sign of recent improvement.

That figure does not include 2021 US Open champion Emma Raducanu and Jack Draper, who both missed out with long-term injuries.

"We obviously want more and more competitors in the second week of Slams - just like the British public," said LTA chief executive Scott Lloyd.

"But the fact we've had four different British players make Grand Slam semi-finals since 2021 - you have to go back 30 years before Andy Murray to have four - shows there is no question that the direction of travel has improved.

"We've just got to keep driving for more - and that's what we're trying to do day in and day out."

Five British men are set to feature in the world top 100 after the US Open, with Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski, Toby Samuel and Jacob Fearnley representing the highest tally since February 2024.

On the women's side, there will be two players - Katie Boulter and Raducanu - in the top 100, although Jones and Harriet Dart moved back to the cusp after reaching the Flushing Meadows second round.

"We've sent 12 players to the world's top 100 over the past eight years and four of those have played Grand Slam semi-finals," said LTA performance director Michael Bourne.

"I'm not sure what other period in the modern era where we've had that level of productivity. Hopefully the number in the top 100 will rise over the next year."

Despite those figures, some will argue that Britain - with its rich tradition and spending power as a Grand Slam nation - is still punching well below its weight.

A glut of injuries for many British players over the past year has not helped the cause.

Former world number four Draper has barely played over the past year because of an arm injury, while Sonay Kartal - who cracked the top 50 last year - has also dropped outside of the top 100 following a long-term back issue.

Britain has fewer players inside the top 100 than the United States, Australia and France, who also benefit from the revenue generated by hosting Grand Slam tournaments.

It also trails nations such as Spain, Italy, the Czech Republic and Argentina, who are all heralded for their talent production.

But Britain cannot simply "pick up a plan" of what others are doing as every country has its own "tennis ecosystem", says Bourne.

Lloyd adds: "We're competing in one of the most internationally elite sports out there and the landscape is vastly different to 40 or 50 years ago in terms of the number of countries which have representation at the top.

"We're ambitious, we want to drive for more, but we honestly believe the indicators are positive. We're moving in the right direction and stronger than where we have been historically."

Encouraging more British children to pick up a racquet from an early age is crucial to developing the next generation of stars.

Draper, Raducanu and Fery - who entered the LTA system at a young age - provide the blueprint.

There are 4.3m juniors playing tennis annually with 1.9m playing every month, which Lloyd says are both all-time records.

But there is a concern that a lack of high-level coaching is stunting the development of many more promising talents.

Bourne admits the UK needs a "higher base" of coaches, adding that one of the LTA's key strategies is "spending time and effort" on developing them.

Chris Marshall, a senior performance coach with over 25 years' experience, fears many youngsters are being priced out of tennis because parents cannot afford quality coaching.

"To fund a 12-year-old at county level right now requires anywhere from £500 to £1,000 a month for coaching, travel, and tournament fees," Marshall, who founded the Young Champs programme to provide free and discounted coaching for children, told BBC Sport.

"It is a massive, stressful financial barrier that makes the sport a non-starter for the vast majority of British families.

"We can't sit around lamenting the lack of British interest in the second week when we are restricting the pipeline that feeds it."

title: York run in five tries for dream win over Catalans
description: York Knights go 10th in Super League as they run in five tries to beat Catalans Dragons in Perpignan.
fullText:

York Knights enjoyed a dream night in the south of France as they ran in five tries to beat Catalans Dragons for the first time in Perpignan.

It looked ominous for the Knights when dashing young Dragons winger Leo Darrelatour crossed inside four minutes, then added a second try for a 10-0 lead on 18 minutes.

But Oli Field pulled one back with his fifth try of the season, improved by Cody Hunter.

And, when David Noafoaluma went in at the left corner, Hunter kicked the goal for a 10-12 lead.

Right on half-time, Darrelatour went almost the length of the field at the Stade Gilbert Brutus for his hat-trick, and Guillermo Aispuro-Bichet kicked his second goal for a 16-12 half-time lead.

But, incredibly, the Dragons then shut out Catalans for the entire second half to earned an eighth league win of the season.

York cheekily took the lead again for the second time on the night on 52 minutes when half-back Liam Harris went 70 yards, then went further ahead on 64 minutes when Scott Galeano went off the right step for his side's fourth try, again improved by Hunter.

And, although they were hampered by a late sin-binning for Jesse Dee, Knights sent their army of travelling fans into French rapture when Paul Vaughan's 79th-minute try completed the scoring.

It completed a first victory for York on their fifth visit to this stadium - their first in Super League - and lifts them up to 10th in the standings, just a place and four points below Catalans.

title: Foxes pain and Burnley suffer hangover - Aaron McLean's EFL takeaways
description: Leicester, Millwall, Swindon, Stoke and Burnley are among the talking points from this weekend's EFL matches.
fullText:
Former Peterborough United and Hull City striker - and Final Score pundit - Aaron McLean gives his five takeaways following Saturday's action in the Championship, League One and League Two.

Questions are already being asked about Russell Martin after Leicester fell to a 4-0 defeat by Oxford United at the King Power Stadium. The Foxes are looking for a return to the Championship at the first time of asking after being relegated last season.

McLean: "I think that it's been difficult for Russell to come into a club that over the past couple of seasons has been on a constant decline and there's been a huge turnover of players.

"His biggest challenge is changing the environment and the mindset of the players. He's also at a club where there's huge pressure being in League One. For a club of that magnitude it's unacceptable.

"So I think it's going to probably take a little bit longer than I'm sure he would like. But at the same time I'm under no illusions, I feel that he is the right man for the job and you just hope that he's given the time to be able to turn things around."

'That's a sackable performance' - what next for Martin at Leicester?

Oxford Utd thump Leicester to heap pressure on Martin

Following a much-needed 4-0 win over high-flying Charlton at the bet365, which lifted them into mid-table, Stoke City are looking to push on after a poor start to the season.

McLean: "A brilliant result for Stoke up against Charlton who potentially could've gone top of the league today after having a great start themselves.

"I think that was a real statement of intent, the manner in which they beat them and that's back-to-back wins for them now, first against a Norwich side that I feel haven't got going yet but will do and a Charlton side who've had a good start to the season.

"I think the recruitment has been good in the summer. Ethan Galbraith was a brilliant signing for them, and hopefully they can continue to build and start to fulfil some of the promise that we've expected from them for the past few seasons."

Stoke hit four to end Charlton's unbeaten start

Alex Neil's Millwall are one of the most unpredictable clubs in the top four divisions. After five games the Lions have lost two matches and won three, including Saturday's emphatic 4-0 victory over Bolton at The Den, which also saw two late red cards.

McLean: "Millwall never seem to draw. They had a brilliant start to the season, wining their first two games then back-to-back defeats, but they're very much back on the horse today after a magnificent performance.

"I fully expect them to be in the shake up at the end of the season. I think that they are a team where it's all or nothing. They will win plenty of games and they will lose a few along the way, but I think that they've got more than enough in the squad to be competing."

Late Dykes double seals Millwall win over Bolton

Burnley sit bottom of the Championship, having been playing against the giants of English football in the Premier League less than six months ago. Their hopes of a first win of the season were squashed late on with Bristol City scoring two goals in the final 10 minutes at Turf Moor.

McLean: "They need to find some kind of cohesion and togetherness at the moment. They just look like a team that's been relegated and a team that is still suffering from the hangover of last season.

"Obviously with a new manager [Nicky Hayen], he needs to get his message across to the boys as he needs to get some kind of confidence into them, but the only way they're going to do that is by sticking together and grinding out a result.

"I think once they get their first win on the board and start to get a little bit of confidence they have got good players in their squad. I think Hayen needs to be given a bit of time. It's far too early in this season to be making decisions on a manager's future."

Bristol City hit late winner to leave Burnley bottom

Ian Holloway has got Swindon Town flying in League Two. They currently sit second behind Bristol Rovers with three wins in their past four matches, with Aaron Drinan's hat-trick securing a 3-1 home victory over Colchester on Saturday.

McLean: "I'm confident that Swindon will do really well this season. I think they'll be really disappointed that they didn't make the play-offs last year. They just missed out and hit a really bad patch of form at the wrong time.

"But I think with a striker like Aaron Drinan, who got a hat-trick today and scored 22 league goals last season, I expect him to probably get even more than that this season. And with the experience they had from last year, I expect them to be fully challenging for automatic promotion this season."

Aaron McLean was speaking to BBC Sport England's Ben Marvell.

title: Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble
description: Taylor Fritz and Flavio Cobolli lose in the third round as six top-10 seeds are knocked out of the men's singles in the first week at the US Open.
fullText:
Taylor Fritz was unable to explain how he let a two-set lead slip against Francisco Cerundolo as he became one of six top-10 seeds to be eliminated from the men's draw in the first week of the US Open.

The American ninth seed was in complete control and went an early break up in the third set, only for Argentina's Cerundolo to produce a shock 3-6 4-6 6-3 6-4 6-4 win to reach the fourth round.

Less than an hour later, fifth seed Flavio Cobolli of Italy fell to a 7-6 (7-4) 3-6 0-6 3-6 defeat by Belgium's Alexander Blockx, opening up the men's draw even further.

"I don't even know what to say," Fritz said. "I don't really want to talk to anybody, see anybody.

"I need to get out for a couple days and then get back to work. I don't know how I let that happen today."

Cerundolo and 28th seed Blockx will now meet in the fourth round with a place in the quarter-finals up for grabs.

This year's biggest shock at Flushing Meadows was also the first, as Novak Djokovic was beaten by Argentina's Mariano Navone on the opening day's play.

Fourth seed Djokovic was eyeing an historic 25th Grand Slam title but was left in tears after a five-set loss to the world number 49.

Next to go was 10th seed Arthur Fils. The Frenchman was another first-round casualty as he went down in four sets against former world number three Stefanos Tsitsipas of Greece.

The highest seed ousted thus far is Canada's Felix Auger-Aliassime, the third seed, who lost to Karen Khachanov in round two, the same stage at which sixth seed Alex de Minaur was beaten.

Those exits looked to have cleared the way for Fritz and Cobolli to go deep into the tournament, but it was an opportunity neither were able to take.

For Fritz, a finalist at Flushing Meadows in 2024, the frustration is all the greater at his home Slam.

He was bidding to become the fifth American through to the fourth round at this year's tournament. With no Jannik Sinner to contend with and Carlos Alcaraz only recently returned from a wrist injury, excitement was growing that, 23 years on from Andy Roddick's US Open triumph, there may finally be another home winner in the men's singles.

That chance persists - but Fritz will know he has let a golden opportunity slip.

Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory

Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open

The chance of a maiden Grand Slam title has also escaped Cobolli for another few months after his capitulation against Blockx.

Having edged the first set on a tie-break, the Italian lost his way and after surrendering the third set to love in just 20 minutes, could not recover.

"I think my energy was a little bit lower than the other days," he said. "I feel a little bit more tight and maybe more tired."

Cobolli admitted Blockx deserved the win and would support him in the next round.

"Alex is very good guy outside the court. He deserved to win, and he won," he added.

Defeats for Cobolli and Fritz mean that apart from top seed Alexander Zverev, only two top-20 players remain in the top half of the draw in 14th seed Learner Tien and 17th seed Jakub Mensik - and they play one another on Friday.

It means Zverev could feasibly reach the final without playing a top-10 player and will not have to face anyone in the top 20 before the semis.

In the men's doubles, British pair Arthur Fery and Joshua Paris progressed with a 6-4 5-7 6-4 win over Anirudh Chandrasekar of India and Ivan Liutarevich of Belarus.

Britain's Neal Skupski and American partner Christian Harrison, the fifth seeds, also advanced as they beat French duo Arthur Reymond and Luca Sanchez 6-0 7-6 (7-3).

But there was disappointment for David Stevenson and Marcus Willis as they lost 5-7 7-6 (7-2) 6-3 to France's 11th seeds Sadio Doumbia and Fabien Reboul.

title: Fans boo as MVP wins in underwhelming UFC farewell
description: Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ends in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris.
fullText:
Michael 'Venom' Page's last fight on his UFC contract ended in an underwhelming win against Nursulton Ruziboev amid booing fans in Paris.

London's Page, who is nicknamed 'MVP', landed a handful of eye-catching strikes during the contest but could not deliver the knockout that the fans craved as he won by unanimous decision.

The 39-year-old's victory means all five of his wins in the UFC since joining in 2024 have come via decision.

Page joined the UFC with a reputation as an innovative striker with a resume of highlight-reel knockouts, but admitted pre-fight he has underperformed since joining the organisation.

Page said the fight with Uzbekistan's Ruziboev was "important to re-establish myself with the UFC", but he did not get the finish he wanted.

Page, who arrived in the UFC over two years ago with 13 knockouts to his name, received a raucous ovation from the French crowd as he entered the octagon.

Ruziboev controlled the majority of the first round on the ground before Page started to open up midway through the fight.

He landed a kick to Ruziboev's knee which wobbled the 32-year-old, before smiling and showboating as he delivered a number of feints.

Page delivered an overhead right and an elbow, but the explosive moments were few and far between as the crowd grew frustrated at a lack of action.

Throughout the bout, Page landed only 12 significant strikes to Ruziboev's eight.

Page has shown throughout his UFC career he is a master of movement and evasion, without having the finishing instinct that the most successful fighters possess.

The fight against Ruziboev followed the same pattern, and although Page was awarded victory by the judges, his arm was raised after jeers from the crowd.

With Page now a free agent, potential options for him if he does not re-sign with the UFC include joining the PFL or turning to boxing.

In the main event, French-Moroccan Salahdine Parnasse earned a stunning first-round TKO win over Dan Hooker.

Parnasse was making his UFC debut and delivered in front of a home crowd, landing a punishing kick to the body before dropping New Zealand's Hooker with a left hook.

The 28-year-old followed with a flurry of punches as Hooker, ranked 12 in the lightweight division, shelled up on the floor, forcing the referee to wave off the contest.

There was also victory for fellow Briton Kurtis Campbell, who submitted American Trevor Peek in the third round of their featherweight bout via a rear-naked choke.

It was a return to winning ways for the 24-year-old Liverpudlian, who lost on his UFC debut to Danny Silva in March.

Campbell's win extends his professional record to nine wins and one defeat.

"I know my debut didn't go the way I wanted it to but I'm here to show I'm the real deal and the future is bright," said Campbell.

Earlier on the card, London's Nathaniel Wood lost by unanimous decision to Moldova's Pavel Andrusca, bringing his four-fight win streak to an end.

Andrusca, who was a late replacement after Wood's original opponent Mairon Santos withdrew 10 days prior to the fight, extended the unbeaten start to his career to nine.

At UFC 322 on 3 October in Salt Lake City, it was announced Brazil's Natalia Silva will fight for the vacant flyweight title against China's Wang Cong.

Former title holder Valentina Shevchenko has vacated the belt and is set to miss over a year with injury, according to the UFC.

title: Wrexham boss Parkinson says Swansea captain should have seen red
description: The Wrexham boss claimed the Wales international's challenge on Callum O'Hare was a 'leg-breaker'
fullText:
Wrexham manager Phil Parkinson says Swansea City captain Ben Cabango got away with a "leg-breaking challenge" in their Welsh derby stalemate.

Parkinson claimed the Wales defender should have been given a straight red for the lunge on midfielder Callum O'Hare late on in the match at the Swansea.com Stadium.

Cabango, who had come on as a second-half substitute, was booked for the foul that prompted an angry reaction from the visitors' bench.

O'Hare was replaced soon after as Swansea maintained their unbeaten start to the season to stay top of the early Championship table.

"I know we want to protect our players but, when someone flies in at that speed, that could have been a leg-breaking challenge," Parkinson said.

"I thought the referee handled the atmosphere well, but in the big decision he didn't make the right call.

"I don't think anybody in the ground or whether people watching back on TV can deny that."

Swansea stay unbeaten but are frustrated by Wrexham in Welsh derby

Eyes on big prize as Swansea and Wrexham collide

More to come from Swansea, insists Matos

Cabango missed the ball in the 77th minute challenge and caught O'Hare, who was making his debut after a £6.5m deadline day move from Sheffield United.

Swansea boss Vitor Matos did not want to get involved in the debate after the game, saying: "I never comment on ref decisions, in one way or the other. If he [Parkinson] says that, good for him."

O'Hare claimed Cabango should have been sent off, saying the 16-cap centre-back told him he "didn't touch" the midfielder.

Parkinson added: "Cabango grabbed Kieffer around the neck on the halfway line before that. A yellow card and then the tackle.

"The same referee has sent Callum Doyle off against Oxford last season for a tackle, which maybe he was slightly out of control.

"But I'm very interested to ask the referee when he compares both those incidents. How he differentiates between the two, because every year, managers have to sit and listen to the referees about what they deem to be red cards, and when you're out of control, like Ben Cabango was and endangering a player. That is a straight red card."

Wrexham still had chances to win the game, but Parkinson said he was pleased with the efforts of his side on the back of a first win of the season, Wednesday's midweek triumph at Millwall.

"I thought we'd got better as the game went on and you know, we looked at an experienced team with a lot of football intelligence to like," said Parkinson, whose side welcome Burnley on Tuesday before a trip to West Ham United on Friday.

"You've got to stay in games with the offensive kind of bravery in situations, but also concentration levels and I thought in the last two games we've done that really well and we can take a lot of credit for that."

title: Humphries beats Greaves as Littler also wins
description: Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour.
fullText:
Luke Humphries and Luke Littler came through their second round matches to progress at the Czech Open on the European Tour.

Humphries ended the challenge of Beau Greaves, who had become the first woman to win a match on the European Tour with her first round win over Daryl Gurney.

The world number two averaged nearly 109 as he beat the three-time women's World Matchplay champion 6-2 in Prague.

"She's an amazing player, she pushed me all the way, it was a couple of bits towards the end of the match that got me through in the end," said Humphries, who will play Andrew Gilding in the third round.

"She's just a great dart player. If I had lost today, I wouldn't have been disgraced, I would have lost to a really great dart player."

World number one Littler had missed the last eight events on the European Tour and marked his return with a 6-4 victory against Germany's Niko Springer.

Littler, who won the men's World Matchplay title in July but was beaten by Brendan Dolan in the semi-finals of a Players Championship event last month, had a 108.59 average in his win.

"It's been a while since I've been to a European Tour," said Littler, who will next play Krzysztof Ratajski.

"Full credit to Niko. I was 5-2 up and then suddenly it was 5-4 and he was right back in it.

"I've just produced a 108 average, but when I was practising backstage I couldn't hit anything."

Michael van Gerwen and Gian van Veen also reached the last 16 with respective wins against Mario Vandenbogaerde and Jeffrey de Graaf.

title: Jones stuns Trump to set up final against Selby
description: Jak Jones earns a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open, and will face Mark Selby in the final.
fullText:
Jak Jones earned a surprise win against Judd Trump at the British Open and will face Mark Selby in the final.

Jones produced breaks of 95 and 68 on the way to a 3-1 lead before Trump levelled the match at 3-3.

However, Jones knocked in a 59 and a 52 to go 5-3 in front and, after England's Trump missed a green on the colours in a lengthy ninth frame, the Welshman secured victory.

"I started off quite well before the interval and then after that I started missing a few, didn't I?" Jones, beaten finalist in the 2024 World Championship, told Channel 5.

"I can't say I'm in this position a lot so it's a bit different for me compared to Judd."

Meanwhile, Selby came through a hard-fought win against fellow Englishman Liam Highfield, who was playing in his first ranking event semi-final.

Highfield took the opening frame before Selby levelled with an 85 and moved into a 3-2 lead.

A 56 helped Highfield level at 3-3, but Selby took three frames in a row to secure a 6-3 victory and a place in his 40th ranking event final.

"It was a tough match, Liam didn't make it easy for me at all," said Selby, who can climb from fourth to second in the rankings if he wins the title.

"His safety was incredible. I can't remember him playing a poor safety shot all the way through the match."

He added: "To think, when I was starting out, a 16-year-old kid in 1999, if somebody had said I'd get to 40 ranking finals, I'd have said 'no chance'. I'd have been happy to get to just one or two."

title: Gauff wins but mixed fortunes for home hopes at US Open
description: Coco Gauff reaches the US Open fourth round but last year's finalist Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys go out on a mixed day for home hopes.
fullText:
Coco Gauff marched into the fourth round of the US Open but compatriots Amanda Anisimova and Madison Keys exited on a mixed day for home hopes in New York.

Gauff, the most recent American champion in New York in 2023, did not have things all her own way but maintained her bid for a second triumph by overcoming Spain's Cristina Bucsa 6-3 6-4.

However, Keys said she felt "scared" as she slumped to defeat despite leading her third set against China's Zheng Qinwen 5-0, while last year's runner-up Anisimova lost in straight sets.

There could yet be as many as five American women in the last 16, with Iva Jovic hoping to join Gauff, Jessica Pegula, Taylor Townsend and Emma Navarro in the fourth round.

American players could also contest six of the eight fourth-round matches in the men's draw, with Ben Shelton, Frances Tiafoe, Tommy Paul and Alex Michelsen through - and Learner Tien and Michael Zheng still to play.

Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory

Fritz and Cobolli shocked as men's seeds tumble

Despite the weight of expectation that she has had to deal with from a young age at her home major, the 22-year-old Gauff is through to the second week at the US Open for a fifth successive year.

Gauff, who became the first American teenager to win the US Open since Serena Williams in 1999 with her breakthrough major success three years ago, heads into the fourth round as the form player in the women's game.

Victory over Bucsa was the 2025 French Open winner's eighth straight-set WTA Tour-level win in a row.

The fourth round is where Gauff's US Open challenge ended in the previous two editions, and she admitted that she struggled to handle the pressure last year.

But in recovering from a 3-1 deficit in the first set, and producing an immediate response to being broken to love in the second, Gauff demonstrated she is better placed to cope with that this time.

"I feel like I'm used to getting to the second week now. I woke up today and I was like 'oh we're already in round three'," Gauff said.

"There's expectations, being American, and I want to do well in front of the fans.

"Last year, I put so much pressure on myself. I'm enjoying the experience out here."

Keys appeared on course for a first fourth-round appearance at her home slam since 2023 after taking a commanding third set lead against Olympic champion Zheng.

But the 2025 Australian Open winner would miss a match point and lose each of the final seven games in a 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 loss that stunned the crowd.

The 31-year-old Keys said she felt as though she "couldn't play tennis anymore" in the final set.

"I obviously got off to a really good lead, and then I got really scared, like I couldn't swing [the racquet]," Keys said.

"I felt like I couldn't play tennis anymore. It just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden."

Keys, who lost the 2017 US Open final to fellow American Sloane Stephens, went out in the fourth round at the other three majors in 2026.

"I feel like I've been struggling for a while now. I'm going to have to make some sort of changes," Keys said.

"I just kind of keep putting it off because that's how the tennis world works. It's just to the point where I actually need to do something about it."

Anisimova, beaten by world number one Aryna Sabalenka in last year's US Open final, lost in straight sets to Russian-born Austrian 24th seed Anastasia Potapova.

The 25-year-old was visibly frustrated with herself throughout the contest, losing her serve twice in the first set and four times in a topsy-turvy second.

title: Seven points from three games - are Hull on track to avoid relegation?
description: It might be too early to settle survival talk, but newly promoted Hull City have given themselves the perfect platform to build on in the Premier League.
fullText:
"Maybe expect to fight for a Champions League place?"

Sergej Jakirovic could not resist a joke when asked about Hull City's remarkable start to life back in the Premier League on BBC Match of the Day.

"No, of course it is early," the head coach was quick to follow up.

Three games into a season is indeed too small a sample size to predict a club's fortunes.

But with seven points from a possible nine, three clean sheets and only two points behind early pacesetters Manchester City, the Hull supporters can be forgiven for dreaming a little.

"It's huge for our confidence coming up into the Premier League," defender John Egan told Sky Sports.

"The start is important. We got the win the first day [against Manchester United] and I think that gave everyone confidence."

If history is anything to go by, the Tigers may already have gone a long way towards securing their most important objective of the 2025-26 season - preserving their top-flight status.

No newly promoted side has been relegated after taking seven or more points from their opening three Premier League games. Looking beyond promoted sides, only three teams have gone down after doing so.

It might be far too early to settle any survival talks but, following another impressive outing in a 0-0 draw against Aston Villa on Saturday, there is no doubting Hull have given themselves the perfect platform to build on.

As recently as last year Hull avoided relegation to League One only on goal difference.

Fast-forward 16 months and they are now going toe to toe with the big names of the Premier League.

The turnaround can be traced back to the arrival of Jakirovic before last season.

The former Bosnia international joined a club under a transfer embargo, confining them to free transfers and loans, but still made them promotion contenders.

Jakirovic guided Hull to a play-off win against a Millwall side who finished three places and 10 points above them, before Oli McBurnie's last-gasp winner against Middlesbrough secured top-flight football.

And Hull did not stay still in the summer.

They were the busiest Premier League side with 18 new signings for about £150m, with six of them, including £22m midfielder Tim Iroegbunam from Everton, arriving on deadline day.

"I know the core of my team. This is the Championship players," said Jakirovic, who signed a two-year contract extension on Friday.

"We brought the players in to put some quality there.

"The big problem for me is who didn't have a pre-season. This is a very big problem. But we will try.

"For example, on Tuesday [against Sunderland in the Carabao Cup], we will use that to give minutes, and at the end they will get a new chance."

The result? Hull have beaten Michael Carrick's United and fellow promoted side Coventry City before holding Europa League winners Villa.

Defensively, they have been outstanding.

Only Charlton in 1998-99 and Huddersfield Town in 2017-18 had kept clean sheets in each of their first three league games after promotion to the Premier League.

"The work goes into it on the training pitch," said Egan, who is part of the three-man defence, alongside Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy, that has yet to be breached.

"It probably started in the play-offs when we moved to that shape. We have a lot of experience and it all helps.

"We've got a lot of lads who want to work together, defend for each other, and so far, so good. We just have to keep improving."

Hull are also comfortable without possession.

No team has had less of the ball this season than Hull (29%). Since 2003-04, only West Ham in 2023-24 (27%) have had a lower figure over their first three matches.

Hull's rise is in stark contrast to last season's Championship winners Coventry, who are yet to open their account after three games.

Only one of the previous 12 promoted sides have survived after doing so - Southampton in 2012-13.

Yet Jakirovic knows Hull's work is far from done.

Wolves in 2011-12, West Brom in 2017-18 and Leeds United in 2022-23 are the three teams who were relegated despite collecting seven points from their opening three matches.

That equates to only 4% of the 78 teams to have collected seven points after three games and still go down.

It might be a low probability, but Hull do not want to take any chances.

"This is a great result for us," Jakirovic said after his side threatened to claim all three points in the closing stages against Villa at MKM Stadium.

"Seven points. Three games. Clean sheet. Let's move on.

"Our goal is to collect the points. I think around 38-40 points, so as soon as possible to get these points."

title: From chess to battle for pole, Gasly has Russell covered at Monza
description: Pierre Gasly delivered the biggest surprise pole position in F1 for years in Italy as the leading contenders had scrappy qualifying sessions.
fullText:
A quarter of an hour before the qualifying session which delivered the biggest surprise pole position in Formula 1 for years, Alpine's Pierre Gasly was playing online chess with Mercedes driver George Russell and winning.

"I must say before the quali, I felt pretty confident," the Frenchman said, "because I was picking piece by piece after piece."

Gasly's performance coach Ben Thorne was watching.

"For a fun story," Gasly said, "Ben told me, 'OK, well, you're getting George here, but he's going to get you in a few minutes.'"

Gasly said he reacted with a swear word but he was smiling as he recalled the moment.

"Turned out that it worked out well. So yeah, it's been fun," he added.

Russell, who lines up second to Gasly, was laughing about it. "He beat me there," the Briton said, "and I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying,' and here we are, he's ahead of me again."

No-one - especially not Gasly nor his Alpine team - would have predicted the 30-year-old would end up on pole in Monza on Saturday, even though his only win in F1 came at this exact track six years ago.

That victory, in the middle of F1's bizarre, spectator-less pandemic season, owed a lot to luck - a remarkable race that ended up with Gasly, then driving for Red Bull's Toro Rosso team, taking a restart from third place and Lance Stroll going off ahead of him on the first lap to gift him the lead once Lewis Hamilton had served a penalty.

This pole was not like that. It was absolutely earned on merit.

The Alpine has strong straight-line speed with a low-downforce-leaning aerodynamic design. The car - which has a Mercedes engine, the best in the field - has looked quick all weekend. It had an upgrade that lifted its performance at the last race in the Netherlands. And Gasly and his team absolutely nailed qualifying, while all the usual leading contenders had scrappy sessions one way or another.

"Monza is a bit of unique track as we know," Gasly said. "It definitely exceeded all our expectations.

"Since this morning, the pace has been better. We managed to make a good step from P3 to quali and I think slightly bigger than the other guys around us.

"Straight from Q1, we were a bit surprised to see us up there. Our target was Q3. But then I was P1 in Q1, then P4 in Q2. I didn't want to get too excited but then first run in Q3, I was third again.

"And then I felt, 'OK, well, I really have a shot at it.' It's probably the first time I really get a true chance and tried to leave everything I had out there.

"It was quite hectic through Ascari and Parabolica. I don't think there was definitely much (left) in there. And crossing the line, I knew it will be one of these laps that will be rewarded. But to the point to get to the pole position, I didn't expect that."

Alpine's Gasly beats Russell to stunning Monza pole

Gasly is well liked within the paddock, and has many friends among the drivers, but he has long been one of F1's forgotten heroes, regardless of that win six years ago.

A Red Bull protege, his time in the works team in 2019 did not work out. Like so many since, he was crushed by Max Verstappen, and demoted back to the second team after half a season.

After sticking with Red Bull for three more years, he was given an opportunity with Alpine, and he hoped a move to a factory team would be his making.

But Alpine have stumbled since, until finally showing signs of a revival this season, following Renault's decision to abandon its F1 engine project and switch to Mercedes customer engines.

The team had been making headlines already this weekend.

On Friday, Gasly lost the podium at Monaco to which he had been promoted after Alpine won an appeal against two penalties for pit-lane speeding, when the FIA court of appeal reinstated the punishment.

A few hours later, de facto team boss Flavio Briatore caused an eruption in a news conference when he alleged one of the four judges in the case had "links" with McLaren.

It was a claim that appeared to lack any substance, based as it was on a charity event in California in 2018 at which the judge in question had been present and to which a local McLaren garage had apparently donated "two or three" cars.

And Briatore provided no evidence to back up the insinuation he was making.

The claim was described as "insulting" in that news conference by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, and afterwards it became clear that McLaren were furious about what Briatore had said on apparently the most flimsy of bases.

Then, on Saturday, a rare statement from the FIA court of appeal refuted the allegation and any "questions (about) the independence and impartiality of the judges".

The court of appeal verdict made a lot of sense. It left many questions about the controversy of the pit-lane penalties in Monaco, but at least it ensured all drivers who had been given them had been treated equitably - notwithstanding the fact that it seems none of them should have received the penalties.

Regardless of the questionable nature of Briatore's comments, Alpine were unhappy about losing their Monaco podium, feeling that they had been given two penalties unjustly when their evidence showed Gasly had never been over the pit-lane speeding limit.

Managing director Steve Nielsen told Sky Sports: "Two or three days ago, we were on the floor. It is really from being down to being on top of the world in just two days and it is amazing. We need to soak it up and make the best of it.

"Pierre is a class act. If you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year.

"We haven't always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have, he has delivered, particularly earlier in the season, So to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful."

In qualifying, Gasly was positioned second last in the train of cars on the final qualifying run, the absolute optimum place in terms of a slipstream.

Others, meanwhile, were compromised in one way or another, including the favourite for pole, Russell, when Verstappen disrupted Mercedes' attempts to have team-mate Kimi Antonelli tow the Briton by getting between the two silver cars at the end of their out laps.

"We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," Russell said. "He wanted to go for the tow, Kimi was there as well, and I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal.

"It takes nothing away from what Pierre achieved because, as he said, they were flying all day, quickest in Q1 and right up there from the beginning. So I'm happy for Pierre and, of course, disappointed we weren't on pole ourselves. However, great place to start for tomorrow."

Russell acknowledged after qualifying what is at stake for him on Sunday. He goes into the race 59 championship points behind leader Antonelli, who has pretty much had his measure all season. But he has a golden opportunity to make up ground on the Italian, who is due to start 20th because of a grid penalty for exceeding his engine allowance.

Russell said: "The win is going to be very important tomorrow but I'm more pleased about the performance. Since the summer break, every lap I have been in the top three positions, while I had that tough run of form before the break when every lap wasn't in the top five."

Antonelli is expected easily to get back into the top six or so, but that would still allow Russell to make a substantial dent in his advantage.

Given Russell has his own grid penalty looming within a couple of races for the same reason, it is imperative for his title hopes that he does so.

Race start at 14:00 BST on Sunday

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra 2; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

On Friday, Gasly did not appear to have the race speed to challenge the top teams, so even though overtaking is harder at Monza than might be expected given its long straights, he knows it will be tough to win the race.

"Obviously not to the pace of these guys around us, but we seem to have picked up more pace from yesterday to today," Gasly said. "So we'll obviously give our best shot and see what we can get out of it."

Aside from Gasly, Russell's main opposition is likely to come from Ferrari, who for the third race in a row seemed to fumble a better qualifying result for operational reasons. It was a bad time to do it again, as they debuted their upgraded engine at their home race.

After both cars came perilously close to being knocked out in the second part of qualifying, Charles Leclerc left the pits in the final session while Lewis Hamilton had no wheels on his car, so the seven-time champion was far from best placed for his run in terms of the slipstream.

Leclerc and Hamilton will start third and fourth after McLaren's Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Red Bull's Liam Lawson.

Hamilton - like Russell, 59 points behind Antonelli - seemed to imply after qualifying that he felt the team should prioritise his hopes over Leclerc's, even if he could not quite bring himself to say it outright.

"(Piastri's penalty) puts us in (with a) fighting chance, hopefully, with George," Hamilton said. "That's one Mercedes up front, so hopefully that gives us a chance to work as a team to try and topple them.

"We're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed.

"So yeah, we do have to work as a team. Have we been... if and when that would ever change... we'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can."

title: How Man Utd plan to compete at top with richer rivals
description: Manager Michael Carrick and chief executive Omar Berrada are united in their viewthat  Manchester United can be successful despite the club's relatively low summer spending.
fullText:
Manchester United believe they can challenge for major honours despite being unable to match the spending power of their rivals.

United spent £148m on new players this summer, less than newly promoted Ipswich, the £300m-plus invested by Chelsea and Tottenham and the record £458m spent by Manchester City.

In their victory at Ipswich on Friday night, Liverpool fielded three players, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, who each cost more than £100m.

Head coach Michael Carrick says money in itself is not the answer to building a successful side and is adamant the club can compete.

"I certainly feel we can," he said. "The challenge is getting the right dynamics, the right balance and the right group together; getting the best players in the group to enhance the rest. Whether you need experience, or some younger players."

There has been some criticism of United's transfer approach, with the lack of a left-back to compete with Luke Shaw and no striking support for Benjamin Sesko two areas highlighted.

Carrick has rejected the notion restrictions have been placed on summer spending by United's hierarchy.

"The actual amount of money I understand can be a big thing but it doesn't always have to be the answer," he said.

Has United's debt has restricted the club's spending power?

Questions about that issue were raised at the Fans Forum at the end of June and respected finance blogger Swiss Ramble estimated in September 2025 that United had paid £852m in interest alone since the Glazer family's takeover in 2005.

The club's latest quarterly figures showed total borrowings of £1.29bn, including outstanding transfer fees.

United also took on an additional £91.92m when refinancing bonds in June and are yet to outline how they will fund a proposed new stadium expected to cost more than £2bn.

The club's full year accounts to 30 June are due out in the next few weeks and will show the latest picture after a season without any European football.

Against that backdrop, fans continue to protest against the Glazers at virtually every match. Yet chief executive Omar Berrada insists the club can remain competitive while managing its debt and stadium ambitions, arguing United's challenge is to operate sustainably while continuing to compete for major trophies.

"We have shown that with debt, we can not only [be] profitable, but more importantly, win trophies," Berrada told the club's Fans Forum on 30 July,. "And our aim is to do that again.

"Our role as management is to be able to operate competitively with a financial structure that's sustainable.

"We also aspire to build a new stadium, but we have to do it in a way that allows us to continue being competitive.

"We need to stay very disciplined and continue to take the right decisions on the pitch and put us in a position where we can do everything, where we can sustain the debt, aspire to build a new stadium and importantly, try to win as many trophies as we can."

The arrivals of Baleba, Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, plus the emergence of 19-year-old forward Shea Lacey leads Carrick to conclude his squad is in a better position now than when they ended last season, when they finished third after winning 12 of his 17 games in charge.

"Being at this club, you've got to strive to win," said Carrick.

"That's where we want to be, and we want to try and get to that on a consistent level.

"I don't like to keep looking back, but they know what it's taken to put that run together. Granted, there was one competition, and we need to do that an awful lot more this season, but we have strengthened the group, so we feel good about what's possible."

Whether that optimism is justified will become clearer over the coming months, but Carrick believes United have assembled a squad capable of challenging despite spending significantly less than many of their rivals.

title: Glasner and Williams dispute VAR call over Forest handball
description: Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner and Neco Williams believe VAR should not have ruled out defender's goal against Tottenham.
fullText:
Nottingham Forest manager Oliver Glasner claimed the video assistant referee (VAR) was "guessing" and should not have intervened in ruling out Neco Williams' goal in their 0-0 draw with Tottenham.

Williams' second-half effort was chalked off with the full-back adjudged to have bundled the ball in with his arm after some calamitous Tottenham defending at the City Ground.

The Forest defender denied it came off his arm and insisted it should have stood.

Initially, referee Craig Pawson awarded the goal but VAR Peter Bankes intervened.

"I watched five or six different angles and, to be fair, from one angle you can guess that the ball touched the arm because the shirt moves a little bit, but it's not clear is it the ball or [Sandro] Tonali on the goalline," said Glasner.

"I think the VAR can't intervene when he is guessing. It was not clear and obvious.

"We had a briefing before the season that the threshold for VAR intervention this year should be very high, which is why this is a wrong intervention.

"If it's not 100% clear, stick to the on-field decisions. This is the inconsistency today.

"I told the referee after the game that I felt the goal should have stood."

The Premier League's official match centre posted on their X page, external the explanation as to why it was ruled out following the incident in the 67th minute.

It stated: "VAR checked the referee's call of goal to Nottingham Forest - and determined that Williams handled the ball immediately before scoring and recommended that the goal was disallowed."

The rule states that if the ball has hit the arm of the goalscorer immediately before they score then it must be ruled out, even if accidental.

However, Williams denied that it struck his arm amid the chaos in the Spurs box.

"It's a goal," the Forest full-back told Sky Sports.

"VAR is there when there is a clear and obvious error and for me that is not clear and obvious. I've seen the images and the replays and at not one moment did I think I handballed it. I headed it in between my arms.

"I knew straight away I've headed it down in between my arms. At a loss at that one. Disappointing."

'Not Football Manager' - De Zerbi says misfiring Spurs need time

The biggest issue with judging handball is often determining if the ball did actually hit the arm, and that is the crux of Forest's argument.

Williams is adamant the ball came off his head and did not touch his hand, evidence which of course would not be available to the VAR.

Even having a chip in the ball, like at the World Cup, would not help here as the head and hands were so close together.

This is not about a clear and obvious error, as that covers subjective incidents like potential penalties.

It is a factual overturn so the VAR, Bankes, is looking for definitive proof. This is similar but without taking into account what the referee, Pawson, says he has seen.

Definitive proof can be seen as a higher bar than clear and obvious, because it is a factual decision - that the ball definitely touched the goalscorer's arm.

Glasner, Williams and most of the Forest fanbase refuse to accept that evidence does exist, and that there were no grounds to disallow the goal.

These decisions come down to one factor - the judgement of who is in the VAR room on a given match.

It is unavoidable that another VAR on a different day might feel the threshold of proof had not been crossed, and allow the goal to stand.

And this will always be one of the major frustrations with VAR.

Harry Maguire's goal against Ipswich last weekend was allowed despite a handball because his shot was going wide before it was deflected, meaning it was an own goal.

In the Williams' case, he actually was the goalscorer so any touch on the arm means the goal must be ruled out.

The only thing that would have saved the goal was if the ball had fully crossed the line before it was kicked against Williams.

title: Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory
description: Zheng Qinwen fights back from 5-0 down in the deciding set and stares down match point to stun American 22nd seed Madison Keys.
fullText:
Zheng Qinwen described her US Open third-round comeback win over Madison Keys as a "very dramatic match" - but that is somewhat of an understatement.

The Olympic champion, who had to come through qualifying to reach the main draw, found herself 5-0 and match point down in the third set against Keys.

But Zheng held firm and reeled off seven games in a row to secure a remarkable 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 victory over the 22nd seed and crowd favourite.

Keys, who won the 2025 Australian Open, appeared to be cruising towards a commanding victory after wrapping up the opening set in just 23 minutes.

But Zheng, who is rebuilding her career after undergoing elbow surgery last year, rallied, clinching it on a tie-break before snatching victory from the jaws of defeat against the American.

Zheng threw herself to the floor in relief and reflected afterwards on a difficult 12 months in which she has questioned if she will rediscover her form.

"Finally, a bit of luck is on my side," the 23-year-old said.

"I am just telling myself ever give up. Somehow, little by little, it's just happened.

"Tennis sometimes feels like rollercoaster. You see many times people have a match point, but at the end we made a comeback."

The Chinese star is the first qualifier to reach the women's fourth round at the US Open since Britain's Emma Raducanu, who went on to win the 2021 title.

Three months ago, Zheng could not hold back her tears in a news conference after a first-round exit at the French Open.

It was her first Grand Slam since undergoing surgery in July 2025 to correct a chronic injury caused by small pieces of bone floating in the elbow.

The injury came after a breakthrough 2024 where she reached the Australian Open final, won Olympic gold and made the US Open quarter-finals.

She had also enjoyed a promising start to 2025 before injury struck, advancing to the last eight at Roland Garros and climbing to a career-high of fourth in the world rankings.

It was understandable, therefore, why Zheng found a first-round defeat in Paris this year difficult to take - even if it was to eventual runner-up Maja Chwalinska after nine months on the sidelines.

Her ranking dropped as low as 160 and she had to contest a Grand Slam qualifying event for the first time in four years.

"After coming back from injury I felt I lost the energy and I forgot how to compete," she said.

Zheng seems to have recaptured some of her best form, having been taken to three sets in four of her six matches in New York so far.

She did not meet criteria for a protected ranking - for which players can apply if they are out injured for at least six months - because she made an early comeback to play her home tournament in Beijing in October 2025.

That meant she had to come through qualifying - something she found difficult to accept.

"I was even crying after I won the third match to reach the main draw," Zheng said.

"The main draw is just the beginning where all the players start. That was my beginning before.

"I fight so hard just to start like everyone else. For me, that was really not easy."

Her composure was on display against Keys - especially at 5-4 0-15 down, when she was forced to stop her service motion after a baby started crying in the crowd.

"If it's adult, probably I will look at him very hard or start to speak, but it's just a baby," Zheng joked.

"I can't do anything, you know? It's just a baby."

Zheng went on to win the next four points to level the tie - and the rest was history.

title: Taylor crowns career in stylish Croke Park triumph
description: Katie Taylor ends illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells.
fullText:
Katie Taylor ended her illustrious career as a three-time undisputed world champion as Croke Park gave one of Ireland's greatest sporting figures the grandest of farewells on a night of celebration, spectacle and music.

The 40-year-old outclassed unbeaten Flora Pili on points in front of 80,000 jubilant fans to add the vacant WBC belt to her WBA, WBO and IBF light-welterweight titles.

With the footwork, speed and sharp pressure fighting that defined her career, Taylor produced one final stylish performance against the overmatched Frenchwoman to win by scores of 100-90, 100-90 and 98-91.

Promoter Eddie Hearn paid tribute to Taylor, calling her "Ireland's greatest sportsperson", before she took one final lap of the ring, waving to the crowd before ceremonially placing her gloves and belts in the centre of the canvas.

After almost a quarter of a century in the sport, Taylor - an Olympic champion, two-weight world champion and one of the pioneers of women's professional boxing - finally got her fairytale ending at her dream venue.

She bows out with a record of 26 wins and just one defeat, but this was about more than one final result.

It was a night steeped in Irish pride, with a spine-tingling atmosphere and chart-topping pop group Westlife helping provide a fitting send-off.

Taylor signs off career in style with unanimous decision win against Pili - reaction

Tears, blood & triumph - Taylor's iconic career in pictures

On an unforgettable night for the city, around 80 per cent of those inside Croke Park had never previously attended a boxing event, but turned out to honour a fighter who dragged women's sport from the margins and took an entire nation on her journey.

The crowd was the sixth largest recorded post-war attendance for a boxing event anywhere in the world. By early evening, the stands were awash with green and white, tricolours draped over shoulders.

Westlife performed 'World of Our Own' and 'You Raise Me Up', with tens of thousands joining in as phone lights flickered around the towering tiers of Croke Park.

The atmosphere softened for an a cappella version of 'Grace', the well-known Irish ballad linked to the 1916 Easter Rising, before the national anthem rang out.

Chants of "Ole, Ole, Ole" drowned out Pili's ringwalk music before Taylor finally emerged to 'All Hail King Jesus', a nod to the faith she has spoken so openly about throughout her career.

She stretched her arms wide, sang along and tried to take in every second of her final walk to the ring. There was emotion on her face, but also the familiar focus as fireworks shot into the Dublin sky.

Taylor had spent fight week insisting there was still a job to do, but even for a fighter who had sold out Madison Square Garden and performed on some of boxing's grandest stages, it was hard to imagine her being untouched by a reception like this.

'One of the best' - boxing world reacts to Taylor's farewell win

After a quiet opener, Taylor - who turned professional in 2016 - burst into life in the second round, firing quick combinations before darting back out of range.

She repeatedly beat Pili to the punch, working in bursts and making the most of the two-minute rounds.

Pili, 29, arrived unbeaten in 12 contests and had previously held the European title. With little expectation on her shoulders, she had everything to gain.

But she had never faced anyone remotely close to Taylor's level and the gulf in class soon began to show.

The party atmosphere continued between rounds as it became increasingly clear there would be no gatecrashing from the Frenchwoman.

Former world champion Prince Naseem Hamed and UFC star Paddy Pimblett watched from ringside as Pili swung wildly in the fifth, only for Taylor to make her miss and fire back.

Pili enjoyed her best spell in the seventh, a quick flurry briefly snapping Taylor's head back, but it did little to alter the direction of the fight.

Croke Park rose for the final two minutes as Taylor continued to press forward, letting her hands go while the noise poured down from the stands.

She embraced her mother, trainer and manager in the ring as 'Celebration' rang around Croke Park before the inevitable result was read out.

"Let me just look around for a second", she said afterwards, soaking up every ounce of the reception.

Taylor has been unequivocal that Croke Park would be the end and she walks away having beaten every opponent she faced as a professional.

Her only defeat came against Chantelle Cameron in Dublin in 2023. Six months later, Taylor returned to the 3Arena and avenged it to become undisputed champion in a second weight division.

After the final bell, she paid tribute to her family and somehow held the tears back as she spoke to the crowd.

"There's nothing like an Irish mammy," she said, smiling as she thanked those closest to her.

For a fighter who has never hidden her dislike of media interviews, there was something striking about the confidence with which she walked around the ring, microphone in hand, soaking up the final moments.

"We did it. We brought boxing back to Croke Park. You were with me in London 2012, you were with me with the heartbreak of Rio. You stayed with me when I turned pro," Taylor said.

"I don't know any other country that would sell 80,000 tickets for a female athlete. I'm convinced Ireland is the only country."

Taylor will forever be defined by her trilogy wins against Amanda Serrano and leaves with a staggering list of accolades, but her true impact cannot be measured in statistics alone.

That legacy belongs to the young girl who once pretended to be a boy just to box when girls were not allowed.

She fought tirelessly to get the sport sanctioned in Ireland and included in the Olympics, before going on to conquer both the amateur and professional codes.

The belts will eventually gather dust, but the trail Taylor blazed across the sport will never fade.

description: Some of the biggest names in women's boxing pay tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park.
fullText:
Some of the biggest names in women's boxing have paid tribute to Katie Taylor after the Irish great ended her career with victory over Flora Pili at Croke Park.

Unified lightweight champion Caroline Dubois called Taylor "one of the best to ever do it", while Claressa Shields said the 40-year-old deserved to "ride off into the sunset".

Taylor beat Pili on points in Dublin to become undisputed light-welterweight champion and retires with 26 wins from 27 professional contests, Olympic gold and three undisputed title triumphs across two divisions.

"Thank you so much for paving the way," Londoner Dubois wrote on X. "Wishing you happiness, success and joy for this next season."

Taylor was sharper throughout, repeatedly beating the Frenchwoman to the punch before finishing with one final burst of combinations as the crowd rose to its feet.

American Shields - the self-proclaimed Greatest Woman of All Time - added: "Congrats Katie. Now ride off into the sunset. You deserve it all."

Super-featherweight champion Alycia Baumgardner described Taylor as "a trailblazer who helped set the stage for all of us".

"What a legacy," she wrote. "It's been a privilege watching your journey from the beginning."

Taylor's farewell unfolded in front of more than 80,000 fans in Dublin, with Westlife performing before the main event and Croke Park providing a fitting backdrop to her final night.

Former world champion Carl Frampton said Taylor's relationship with the Irish public was unlike anything else in boxing.

"You can tell that she doesn't enjoy doing stuff in front of the media, but she still has this adulation from everybody," the Northern Irishman said.

"Katie Taylor is different, she's special and there will never be another one like her."

Former cruiserweight world champion Tony Bellew described the occasion as one of the most remarkable exits the sport had seen.

"I don't think in all of my years of watching this game, I have seen an exit as beautiful, amazing and fitting," he said.

"She has just retired as the greatest champion ever. I have never seen a fighter leave as an undisputed champion on their own terms."

Former world champion Barry Jones picked out the final 20 seconds, when Taylor produced the kind of rapid combinations which defined so many of her biggest fights.

"That's what you really remember about her," he said on the Dazn broadcast.

"Those rallies of big punches, combinations and that's how she finished her last fight."

American Mikaela Mayer - who was also ringside - was struck by the final image of Taylor placing her gloves in the centre of the ring.

"I was sitting there watching her put her gloves in the centre of the ring and it's like a story," she said.

Taylor had long dreamed of fighting at Croke Park and had made clear she wanted the stadium to stage the final chapter of her career.

Bellew said there was "no way" Taylor would return to boxing, although he could see her remaining involved by mentoring younger fighters.

"She will always be there to give her advice, speak to her and help her," he said.

"But ultimately she will sail off into the sunset and who could possibly deserve it more."

title: Find a banknote with a ‘solid’ serial number? It’s probably worth so much more
description: Banknotes with "solid" serial numbers have routinely sold for thousands on auction sites — if they're in excellent condition.
fullText:
(NEXSTAR) – Building a collection of unique banknotes? You'd be off to a solid start if you find one with a "solid" serial number.

A "solid" serial number, as known to collectors, is a serial number on a U.S. banknote that features only a single repeating digit, such as "11111111" or "77777777." Bills with such numbers might not be quite as rare as, say, a discontinued banknote or a bill with a double denomination error, but they're still among some of the most recognized "oddities" in paper-money collecting, according to Doug Mudd, the curator and director of the American Numismatics Association's Edward C. Rochette Money Museum in Colorado.

"As a type, they are somewhat popular because they are more readily noticeable," Mudd tells Nexstar.

Mudd pointed out, however, that a "solid" serial number is technically "just as rare or common as any other," mathematically speaking. But much like collectors who seek out "radar" serial numbers (i.e., palindromic numbers, such as 12344321 or 55433455), there are indeed niche collectors willing to pay well over face value for more unique specimens.

In fact, banknotes with solid serial numbers generally fetch more than other so-called "fancy" serial numbers, seeing as there are fewer possible bills with solid numbers in a series.

"Many collectors don't have a solid among their fancy serial number notes," one member of Reddit's r/PaperMoney community remarked in a post about a collector who found a "solid" $20 banknote earlier this year.

"Right place, right time, I guess," the user said.

Archived auction data from Heritage Auctions and Stacks Bowers shows that solid-numbered bills have routinely sold for thousands of dollars apiece, if they're in good condition. Some buyers have also paid premiums for specific solid numbers like 77777777 or 88888888 — numbers thought to be more lucky or auspicious in certain cultures. (A "near-perfect" $100 bill with a solid 8 serial number sold for more than $19,000 in 2024, the Heritage Auction website indicates.)

Imperfect bills with solid serial numbers can still fetch many times their face value, recent eBay sales indicate. An ungraded $1 note with a solid 3 serial number sold for $1,600 earlier this month, while a $5 bill with a solid 2 serial number sold for $2,660 as part of a series with several other bills of sequential serial numbers. The auction platform also appears to be crawling with "near solid" or "almost solid" banknotes for sale (e.g., 44444447 or 91999999), though those were selling for far less.

Mudd, meanwhile, told Nexstar that bills with fancy serial numbers are generally less "interesting" to most paper-money hobbyists or historians, as they aren't exactly anomalies, and don't come with much of a story. But when it comes sheer value, these bills certainly have their buyers.

"[They're] definitely worthwhile to the specialist," Mudd said. "[…] There are people very interested in them and they will pay more money."

Hisahito, the nephew of Emperor Naruhito, is second in line to Japan's 1,500-year-old Chrysanthemum Throne and the youngest of 16 members of the rapidly shrinking and aging imperial family. Robin Morgan, a wholesome child star of the 1940s and '50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died at age 85.

title: Fighter jet crashes at air show, killing 2 pilots with thousands of spectators watching
description: Video captured a Phantom F-4 jet crashing into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver at Tanagra Air Force Base as thousands witnessed it.
fullText:
A day at an air show turned fatal Saturday when a Greek air force jet crashed north of Athens as thousands of spectators watched.

Both pilots were killed in the crash at Tanagra Air Force Base, but no civilians were hurt.

The twin-seat Phantom F-4 jet flew into the ground during a low-altitude maneuver just meters above the ground.

Eight Believed Dead After B-52 Crashes Shortly After Takeoff From Edwards Air Force Base

"The sense of grief is widespread, and our thoughts are with the families of the two pilots we lost," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said. "It is a reminder of the daily danger faced by Greece's aviators, who remain on constant standby to protect Greece's skies."

The jet burst into flames on impact, sending up a large plume of black smoke, prompting 11 water-dropping planes and helicopters to assist 85 firefighters in extinguishing the blaze.

11 Skydivers, One Pilot Killed In Missouri Plane Crash Near Airport

Video of the crash showed a second ball of fire nearby as the plane broke apart.

The bodies of the pilots were eventually recovered.

"We were all stunned. It hadn't been airborne for more than three minutes," an eyewitness told ERT, Greece's state-owned broadcaster.

The crash happened during the country's annual Athens Flying Week.

The organizers canceled the rest of the events after the incident, and the area was evacuated.

"It is with deep sadness that I learned of the death of the two officers of the Hellenic Air Force, who lost their lives in the tragic accident that occurred during the air show at Tanagra Air Base," Cyprus' Defense Minister Vasilis Palmas said, adding he had called Nikos Dendias, Greece's Minister of National Defense.

Air Force Identifies 8 Crew Members Killed In B-52 Stratofortress Crash At Edwards Air Force Base

The air force has declared three days of mourning in the country.

In May, two jets collided during an air show in Idaho, but the pilots were able to safely eject.

The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.
